title: Exploitation of CVE-2024-35250 via Kernel Streaming IOCTL Requests
id: 1a6f7b8c-9d4e-5f6a-7b8c-9d4e5f6a7b8c
status: experimental
description: Detects exploitation of CVE-2024-35250 by monitoring for process creation involving kernel streaming device interactions with specific IOCTL codes and property set IDs used in privilege escalation attempts.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2024/12/cisa-and-fbi-raise-alerts-on-exploited.html
    - https://devco.re/blog/2024/08/23/streaming-vulnerabilities-from-windows-kernel-proxying-to-kernel-part1-en/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-27
tags:
    - attack.privilege-escalation
    - attack.t1068
    - attack.defense-evasion
    - attack.t1211
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY'
            - 'KSPROPSETID_DrmAudioStream'
            - 'KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET'
            - 'KsSynchronousIoControlDevice'
            - 'RequestorMode'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: high

pipeline.attack_summary: Slingshot is a sophisticated APT that compromises Mikrotik routers via Winbox Loader, downloads malicious DLLs like ipv4.dll to victim machines, and uses kernel-mode modules such as Cahnadr/NDriver and GollumApp for persistence, data collection, and exfiltration. It exploits known driver vulnerabilities to load into kernel mode without detection.

indicators.context: The name appears unencrypted in some of the malicious samples – it is the name of one of the threat actor’s components, so we decided to extend it to the APT as a whole.
The initial loader replaces the victim's legitimate Windows library 'scesrv.dll' with a malicious one of exactly the same size.
One of them – ipv4.dll – has been placed by the APT with what is, in fact, a downloader for other malicious components.
In turn, this infected the administrator of the router. We believe this cluster of activity started in at least 2012 and was still active at the time of this analysis (February 2018).
Following infection, Slingshot would load a number of modules onto the victim device, including two huge and powerful ones: Cahnadr, the kernel mode module, and GollumApp, a user mode module.
Canhadr, also known as NDriver, contains low-level routines for network, IO operations and so on.

The most sophisticated module is GollumApp. This contains nearly 1,500 user-code functions and provides most of the above described routines for persistence, file system control and C&C communications.
During our research we also found a component called KPWS that turned out to be another downloader for Slingshot components.
These vulnerabilities include CVE-2007-5633; CVE-2010-1592, CVE-2009-0824.

We were able to find several cases where the attackers got access to Mikrotik routers and placed a component downloaded by Winbox Loader, a management suite for Mikrotik routers.

attack_vector.reasoning: The text clearly describes a phishing email with a hyperlink leading to a download link for the malware. The attack vector is straightforward social engineering followed by execution of a downloaded file.

pipeline.attack_summary: An attacker uses phishing emails containing hyperlinks to deliver a 7z archive with a new NetWire RAT variant. The archive contains an executable that employs anti-analysis techniques like dynamic code extraction and anti-sandboxing. Once executed, the malware relocates itself, establishes persistence via registry keys, collects system information, and communicates with a C2 server using DNS resolution for IP address discovery. It supports over 80 commands including credential theft, file operations, process control, and network monitoring.

indicators.context: The downloaded file is a 7z file, which contains the new variant of NetWire RAT.
After decompressing it, we are able to get an EXE file with the name of "PROFORMA-INVOICE 0990.exe".
The malware file download link is: "hxxps[:]//www[.]mediafire[.]com/file/d86hz5qj21lmhrb/PROFORMA-INVOICE_0990.7z/file".
Its domain is found in the decrypted string, which for this variant is "gbam0001.duckdns[.]org:3366".
The process where NetWire was relocated to "C:\Users\user_name\AppData\Roaming\Install\Host.exe".
NetWire continues to create its home key (HKCU\SOFTWARE\NetWire) as well as adding it into the auto-run group in the victim's registry.
NetWire creates a log folder to store the log files of information that it collects from the victim's system. The log folder is located at "%AppData%\Logs".
It checks to see if the current executable file is located in the correct folder (%AppData%\Install) and has the right file name (Host.exe).
If not, it relocates the file into "%AppData%\Install" and renames it as "Host.exe".
It calls the API USER32.GetCursorPos() twice to obtain two mouse cursor positions and then compares them.
It also calls the API ntdll.ZwGetContextThread to obtain the current thread context structure, which contains the CPU debug register status.
call dword ptr [ebp+110]     ;kernel32.GetCurrentThread
Next, it initializes several global variables and Windows Sockets by calling the API WSAStartup().
Current login User name collected by calling the API GetUserNameA() or from the system environment variable.
Victim's Computer name by calling the API GetComputerNameA().
Victim's Windows version information by calling the API GetVersionExA().
It then calls the _beginthreadex() function to start a thread, the thread function of which registers a window class, whose window procedure function is a keylogger.
Once the connection with its server is established, NetWire starts waiting for the C&C server to reply with a "9B" command packet

Analysis and Report by Fabian Marquardt (@marqufabi) Recently, Telekom Security CTI was made aware via trust groups in which we are engaged about a new malware campaign that is distributed via phishing emails. The malspam campaign used stolen email threads to lure victim users into clicking the contained hyperlink, which downloaded the malware. Attention to this malware campaign was also fueled by a false attribution of one of the malware samples to Emotet. Even though this attribution later turned out as a false positive match of an automated detection rule, it caused the security research community to focus on this new campaign. Initial analysis quickly revealed significant similarity to the DarkGate malware, based on the use of a similar initial infection routine (AutoIt scripts) and the observed C2 communication protocol, which matched past analyses of the same malware family. Further analysis confirmed this initial attribution, since embedded strings and contained functionality clearly identified the sample as part of the DarkGate malware family.

The AutoIt script is bundled with the .au3 file extension which is usually used for plain-text scripts. Instead it contains a pre-compiled script, which would typically use the .a3x extension. We can see that it is a compiled script from the magic bytes AU3!EA06, which for some reason are not at the start of the file, but follow a long sequence of base64-encoded data (we will come back to that below!).

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack begins with unauthenticated access to a Veeam Backup & Replication instance via TCP port 9401, followed by execution of PowerShell scripts through SQL shell commands. The initial payload is POWERTRASH, an obfuscated loader attributed to FIN7, which executes a reflective PE injection. Lateral movement is performed via WMI and SMB, with additional reconnaissance commands like netstat, tasklist, and ipconfig used to gather system information.

id: 9e1a6c7d-4b3f-4e5a-9c2d-1a3b4c5d6e7f
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of the 'net group' command with parameters that create or add users to a group named 'ESX Admins', which is a known technique used by threat actors to exploit CVE-2024-37085 for privilege escalation on ESXi hypervisors.
references:
    - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/07/29/ransomware-operators-exploit-esxi-hypervisor-vulnerability-for-mass-encryption/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/012/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/004/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1529/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-27
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.privilege-escalation
    - attack.t1078
    - attack.t1059.012
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'net group "ESX Admins" /domain /add'
            - 'net group "ESX Admins" * /domain /add'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts that create or manage domain groups named 'ESX Admins'
level: high

title: Raspberry Robin Initial Access via Infected USB Drive with LNK File
id: f8c4d83e-edfa-496f-a840-5dee769262ba
status: experimental
description: Detects the initial access phase of Raspberry Robin worm where an infected USB drive with a LNK file executes cmd.exe to launch msiexec.exe for payload installation from compromised QNAP NAS devices.
references:

    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.003

            - 'msiexec.exe'

falsepositives:

references:
    - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/10/27/raspberry-robin-worm-part-of-larger-ecosystem-facilitating-pre-ransomware-activity/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/010/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/011/

    - attack.t1218.011

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_lolbin:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'regsvr32.exe'
            - 'rundll32.exe'
            - 'odbcconf.exe'
            - 'control.exe'
            - 'fodhelper.exe'
    condition: selection_lolbin
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative tools using LOLBins
level: high

title: Raspberry Robin Persistence via RunOnce Registry Key Modification
id: 42df50c2-8ae1-4b78-a625-b2024377876c
status: experimental
description: Detects the persistence mechanism of Raspberry Robin by monitoring modifications to the RunOnce registry key, which is used to execute malicious code upon system reboot.
references:
    - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/10/27/raspberry-robin-worm-part-of-larger-ecosystem-facilitating-pre-ransomware-activity/

    - Legitimate software using RunOnce for updates or initialization

title: Raspberry Robin Defense Evasion via Disable Windows Defender Removable Drive Scanning
id: ee3c781f-6562-410b-a3ce-8dab89063b7f

author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-27
tags:
    - attack.defense-evasion

    product: windows
detection:

        CommandLine|contains:

The attack chain is well-documented from insertion to execution and persistence mechanisms. While there are references to researcher workflow, the core attack vector is explicitly described.

pipeline.attack_summary: Raspberry Robin is a worm that initially spreads via infected USB drives containing LNK files disguised as folders. Upon insertion, it executes cmd.exe to launch msiexec.exe which installs malicious payloads from compromised QNAP NAS devices. It uses living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) like rundll32.exe and regsvr32.exe for execution and persistence, often adding itself to the RunOnce registry key. The worm has evolved to deploy other malware families such as FakeUpdates, IcedID, Bumblebee, and TrueBot, linking it to larger cybercriminal ecosystems and leading to ransomware deployments.

indicators.context: The code disables Windows Defender's removable drive scanning, likely to avoid detection during malicious activity on external storage devices. This is a common evasion technique used by malware to reduce antivirus interference.

Upon insertion of the infected drive or launching of the LNK file, the UserAssist registry key in Windows—where Windows Explorer maintains a list of launched programs—is updated with a new value indicating a program was launched by Windows. The malware uses cmd.exe to launch msiexec.exe.
Raspberry Robin's LNK file points to cmd.exe to launch the Windows Installer service msiexec.exe and install a malicious payload hosted on compromised QNAP network attached storage (NAS) devices.

Post-exploitation tools include network scanners, lateral movement utilities like BOUNCER (reused from APT1), and a custom PSExec variant for remote command execution.

    - https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/08/25/mercury-leveraging-log4j-2-vulnerabilities-in-unpatched-systems-to-target-israeli-organizations/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/002/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-27
tags:
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.t1078.002
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\cmd.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'net user admin*/add'
            - 'net localgroup Administrators admin /add'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative tasks creating accounts
level: high

title: Potential Atlassian Confluence CVE-2021-26084 Exploitation Attempt
rules_yaml:
title: Initial Access via CVE-2021-26084 OGNL Injection in Confluence
id: 5e3b7c9a-7d8f-4a1b-9e2c-1f4d6e8a9b0c
status: experimental
description: |
    This rule detects initial access attempts exploiting CVE-2021-26084 in Atlassian Confluence Server or Data Center via unauthenticated OGNL injection.
    The attack targets specific endpoints like /pages/createpage-entervariables.action with attacker-controlled query parameters such as 'queryString'.
    It looks for known OGNL injection patterns in the HTTP request URI, which are indicative of exploitation attempts.
references:
    - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-26084
    - https://confluence.atlassian.com/doc/confluence-security-advisory-2021-08-25-1077906215.html
    - https://github.com/h3v0x/CVE-2021-26084_Confluence
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1580/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-27
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.t1190
    - cve.2021-26084
    - attack.t1213
    - attack.t1580
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection_uri:
        cs-uri-query|contains:
            - 'queryString='
            - '${'
            - 'class.module.classLoader'
            - 'exec('
    selection_endpoint:
        cs-uri-stem|endswith:
            - '/pages/createpage-entervariables.action'
    condition: 1 of selection_ *
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative tools or scripts using similar query parameters for legitimate purposes.
level: high

title: Execution Stage Exploitation of CVE-2021-26084 via OGNL Command Execution
id: 9f4a8d0b-6e7c-5b2a-8f3d-2e4c7f9a1b0d
status: experimental
description: |
    This rule identifies the execution phase of CVE-2021-26084 exploitation by detecting OGNL command execution patterns in HTTP request URIs.
    These patterns indicate that an attacker has successfully executed arbitrary commands on the target system through the vulnerable Confluence application.
references:
    - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-26084
    - https://confluence.atlassian.com/doc/confluence-security-advisory-2021-08-25-1077906215.html
    - https://github.com/h3v0x/CVE-2021-26084_Confluence
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1580/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-27
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.007
    - cve.2021-26084
    - attack.t1213
    - attack.t1580
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection_exec:
        cs-uri-query|contains:
            - 'exec('
    condition: selection_exec
falsepositives:
    - Scripts or applications legitimately using OGNL expressions with exec functions.
level: critical
